notes.summary: In fill in the blanks you choose the word, phrase or sentence that best completes a sentence. SSC asks 2 to 4 of these in Tier 1 and more in Tier 2. Blanks test vocabulary (meaning, collocations, phrasal verbs, idioms, homophones) and grammar (prepositions, articles, verb forms, connectors, comparison). Newer papers also give short paragraphs where you choose missing sentences or the order of segments. The method is always the same: find the clue in the sentence, decide what kind of word is needed, then check meaning.

concepts.title: The three-step method
concepts.body:
1. Find the clue word: a word in the sentence that tells you the meaning of the blank. Far from being ___ by the early failures, he became even more determined. Clue: even more determined → the blank means discouraged → daunted.
  2. Decide the grammar: noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition? Cross out options that cannot fit.
  3. Check the fit: put the answer in and read the full sentence. It must sound natural, not just be close in meaning.

concepts.title: Clue words: same direction or opposite
concepts.body:
SignalWordsWhat it tells you
Same directionand, also, moreover, as well as, i.e., because, soThe blank agrees with the clue.
Opposite directionbut, yet, although, despite, however, far from, instead of, unlikeThe blank is the opposite of the clue.
Definitionthat is, which means, a colon (:)The blank is explained right after it.
Examplesuch as, for example, likeThe examples show the meaning.
Example: The speech was so ___ that no one understood what he meant. The result (no one understood) points to ambiguous, not lucid.

concepts.title: Collocations
concepts.body:
Some words naturally go together; others just sound wrong even if the meaning is close.
VerbGoes with
makea decision, a mistake, a fuss, an effort, progress, a promise, money, a profit, a suggestion
dohomework, your duty, business, harm, good, a favour, justice, the dishes
takea risk, care, part, a break, a decision (also correct), place, action, steps
payattention, a visit, a compliment, tribute, heed
giveadvice, a speech, permission, an example, priority
face / bearthe consequences, a challenge
keep / be intouch, a promise, a secret
commita crime, suicide, an error
Adjective + noun: heavy rain, heavy traffic, strong tea, strong wind, high fever, deep sleep, hard-earned money, bitter truth, close friend, fast colour.

concepts.title: Homophones and homonyms
concepts.body:
Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning. Homonyms are spelt the same but have different meanings (a compact mirror = small; signed a compact = an agreement).
PairMeanings
heal / heelcure / back of the foot
dew / duewater drops / expected, owed
blew / bluepast of blow / a colour
route / rootway / part of a plant
grown / groanpast participle of grow / a sound of pain
principal / principlehead of a school, main / a rule or belief
stationary / stationerynot moving / paper and pens
complement / complimentcompletes / praise
council / counsela group / advice
accept / exceptreceive / leaving out
affect / effectto influence (verb) / result (noun)
loose / losenot tight / fail to keep
than / thencomparison / time
peace / piececalm / a part
sole / soulonly, bottom of the foot / spirit
cite / site / sightquote / a place / vision
For which sentence uses the homonym: decide what the word means in the given sentence, then pick the option where the same spelling has a different meaning.

concepts.title: Prepositions after words
concepts.body:
Word + prepositionExample
aware of, afraid of, capable of, fond of, proud of, guilty of, accused ofHe was accused of theft.
charged with, angry with (a person), satisfied with, familiar with, comply withHe was charged with theft.
angry at / about (a thing), good at, surprised atShe is good at maths.
interested in, confident in, succeed in, believe in, rich inHe succeeded in passing.
depend on, rely on, insist on, congratulate on, comment onI insist on paying.
responsible for, famous for, apologise for, eligible forHe apologised for the delay.
different from, prevent from, refrain from, suffer fromRefrain from smoking.
similar to, prefer to, superior to, senior to, junior to, addicted to, apologise to (a person)She is senior to me.
opt for (choose), opt against / out of (decide not to)He opted against the plan.
Time: since + point (since 2015, since Monday); for + period (for two hours). between two, among more than two.

concepts.title: Articles and determiners
concepts.body:
• a before a consonant sound: a university, a European, a one-rupee coin. an before a vowel sound: an hour, an honest man, an MBA, an apple.
  • the for something specific, already mentioned or unique: the sun, the Himalayas, the Ganga, the best student, the absence of data.
  • No article before general plural or uncountable nouns: Water is precious; Books are useful.
  • much, little + uncountable (much time); many, few + countable plural (many books).
  • few = hardly any; a few = some; the few = all of the small number. Same pattern for little, a little, the little.
  • each, every + singular noun and singular verb: Every student has a book.

concepts.title: Verb forms, tense and conditionals
concepts.body:
PatternExample
Zero conditional (always true): If + present, presentIf the protocol is breached, the system alerts the staff.
First conditional: If + present, will + V1If it rains, we will stay in.
Second conditional: If + past, would + V1If I were rich, I would travel.
Third conditional: If + had + V3, would have + V3If he had worked hard, he would have passed.
since / for → perfect tenseI have lived here since 2015.
need not / must / can + V1You need not make a fuss.
look forward to, used to (be accustomed), object to + -ingI look forward to meeting you.
It is time + pastIt is time we left.
Subject-verb agreement: One of the boys is; Neither the manager nor the clerks were (verb follows the nearer subject).

concepts.title: Connectors and comparison
concepts.body:
• than for comparison (easier than); then for time (and then).
  • as… as for equality (as tall as); so… that for result (so tired that); such a… that (such a hot day that).
  • although / though + clause; despite / in spite of + noun. Although is not followed by but.
  • unless = if not; never unless… not.
  • either… or, neither… nor, not only… but also, both… and, hardly / scarcely… when, no sooner… than.
  • Degrees: more spacious than, the most spacious; never more better or most best. Latin comparatives take to: superior to, senior to, prefer X to Y.
  • Adjective describes a noun (a careful driver); adverb describes a verb (drives carefully). Adverbs of frequency (often, always, never, usually) come before the main verb but after be: She often goes; She is always late.

concepts.title: Sentence and segment blanks
concepts.body:
Missing sentences (S1 to S4): S1 and S4 are given, and you pick S2 and S3. S2 must follow on from S1 (often through a pronoun or the same subject) and S3 must lead into S4. Test the options' first sentence against S1, then the second against S4.
Order of segments: a sentence has several blanks and each option gives the segments in a different order. Fill the first blank (it must continue the words before it) and the last blank (it must lead into the words after it), then eliminate.

varieties.name: Word that fits the meaning
varieties.how: Find the clue word in the sentence, decide whether the blank agrees with it or contrasts with it, then pick the option with that meaning.

example.q: Far from being ______ by the early failures, the young scientist became even more determined. (encouraged / daunted / inspired / elated)
steps: Far from signals the opposite of what follows.
He became more determined, so the blank must mean discouraged.
daunted = discouraged.

varieties.name: Collocation
varieties.how: Look at the word right next to the blank. Choose the option that naturally pairs with it, even if other options have a similar meaning.

example.q: Before buying a house, you should ______ a careful decision. (do / make / take out / give)
steps: The noun is decision.
The natural pairs are make a decision or take a decision; only make is offered.

varieties.name: Phrasal verb
varieties.how: Turn each phrasal verb into one plain word, then test it in the sentence.

example.q: The family recipes were ______ from one generation to the next. (passed away / passed in / passed down / passed out)
steps: passed away = died; passed out = fainted; passed in is not a common phrasal verb.
passed down = handed on to younger people.

varieties.name: Idiom in the blank
varieties.how: Translate each idiom into plain words and pick the one that matches the meaning the sentence needs.

example.q: Kalam's house was within easy reach of the temple. It was just ________ from it. (a stone's throw away / at one's fingertips / at arm's length / from pillar to post)
steps: The sentence says the house was very near.
a stone's throw away = very close.

varieties.name: Homonym or homophone
varieties.how: Say each option aloud; they sound alike, so decide by meaning and spelling. For which sentence uses the homonym, find the sentence where the same word has a different meaning.

example.q: The ointment will help to ______ the wound. (he'll / heel / heal / kneel)
steps: The sentence is about curing a wound.
heal = cure; heel = back of the foot.

varieties.name: Preposition
varieties.how: Check whether the word before the blank takes a fixed preposition. If not, apply the time or place rule.

example.q: The shopkeeper was charged ______ selling adulterated food. (of / for / with / on)
steps: charged (with an offence) takes with.
Compare accused of.

varieties.name: Article or determiner
varieties.how: Check the sound of the next word (a / an), whether the noun is specific (the), and whether it is countable (many / few) or uncountable (much / little).

example.q: In ____ absence of reliable data, the decision was postponed. (an / a / the / no article)
steps: absence here is specific: the absence of reliable data.
A noun followed by an of-phrase that makes it specific takes the.

varieties.name: Verb form and tense
varieties.how: Find the subject and the time clues (since, if, yesterday, now). Check agreement and the conditional pattern.

example.q: If the security system ___ breached, it alerts the administrators instantly. (were / is / has / had been)
steps: The main clause alerts is simple present: a general truth.
Zero conditional: If + present, present.
Passive simple present: is breached.

varieties.name: Conjunction or connector
varieties.how: Decide the relation between the two parts (comparison, contrast, condition, reason, result) and choose the connector that shows it.

example.q: Nowadays, online shopping is easier ________ shopping in a market. (like / than / then / as)
steps: easier is a comparative.
A comparative is followed by than; then is about time.

varieties.name: Adjective, adverb or comparison
varieties.how: Ask what the word describes: a noun needs an adjective, a verb needs an adverb. For comparison, check than (comparative), the (superlative) or as… as (equal).

example.q: The house they bought was ______ spacious than their previous house. (most / more / much / very)
steps: than needs the comparative degree.
spacious is a long adjective, so the comparative is more spacious.

varieties.name: Missing sentences in a paragraph
varieties.how: Pick the sentence that follows naturally from S1 as S2, then check that S3 leads into S4. Eliminate options whose first sentence breaks the link with S1.

example.q: S1: Ravi missed the last bus home. S4: He reached home after midnight, tired but safe. P: He decided to walk the six kilometres. Q: The bus driver was his uncle. R: On the way, it started to rain heavily. S: He bought a new car. Choose S2 and S3. (P, R / Q, S / R, P / S, Q)
steps: After missing the bus, he needs another way home: P (he decided to walk).
R (on the way, it rained) continues the walk and leads into reaching home tired.
Q and S do not fit the story.

varieties.name: Order of segments for several blanks
varieties.how: Fix the first blank by what comes before it and the last blank by what comes after it, then check the middle reads smoothly.

example.q: Though Sheela loves horror movies, ____ / ____ / ____ she rented another romantic film today. Segments: A. so much so that B. she tried a romantic film yesterday C. and enjoyed it very much. Options: BCA / ABC / CAB / BAC
steps: After Though… horror movies, the contrast comes first: B.
C continues B: and enjoyed it very much.
A (so much so that) leads into the result: she rented another romantic film.

tips: Read the full sentence before looking at the options; find the clue word first.
Contrast words (but, although, far from, despite) mean the blank is the opposite of the clue.
Cross out options of the wrong part of speech before thinking about meaning.
For prepositions, learn word + preposition pairs as one unit (accused of, charged with).
For homophones, say the options aloud and then check the spelling that matches the meaning.
Read the sentence again with your answer; it should sound natural, not just be close in meaning.
For S1 to S4 questions, link S2 to S1 first and S3 to S4 second; one link usually leaves one option.
traps: Two options with the same meaning where only one collocates (do a decision is wrong; make a decision is right).
a or an decided by the first letter instead of the first sound (an hour, a university).
few and a few have opposite feelings: few friends (hardly any) vs a few friends (some).
A phrasal verb that uses the right verb but the wrong particle (passed away vs passed down).
since with a period of time: it should be for two hours, not since two hours.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The new employee was not aware ______ the office rules.
questions.solution: The adjective aware takes the preposition of: aware of something.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Before buying a house, you should ______ a careful decision.
questions.solution: The natural collocation is make a decision. Do a decision or give a decision (in this sense) is not standard English.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The minister's speech was so ______ that the audience could not understand what he actually meant.
questions.solution: The audience could not understand the meaning, so the speech was unclear: ambiguous (open to more than one meaning). Lucid and concise suggest clarity; candid means frank.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The shopkeeper was charged ______ selling adulterated food.
questions.solution: The fixed phrase is charged with an offence. (Compare: accused of an offence.)

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Far from being ______ by the early failures, the young scientist became even more determined to succeed.
questions.solution: Far from being X … became more determined means she was not discouraged. The blank needs a word meaning 'discouraged': daunted. The other three are positive and break the contrast.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The police have launched an inquiry, and anyone found guilty will have to ______ the consequences.
questions.solution: The standard collocation is face the consequences. Confront with and suffer from add wrong prepositions; meet the consequences is unidiomatic.

flashcards.back: although, but, yet, despite, however, far from
